extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne; readers interested in personal essays, self-reflection, and practical philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: An early-modern personal/philosophical essay exploring conscience, practice, death, self-knowledge, and the nature of honour; mixes anecdote, moral reflection, and classical citation. Useful as a model for self-examination essays and practical moral argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as counterpoison
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience counteracts the delights of vice by producing inward displeasure and tormenting imaginations (dreams, remorses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that at the same time men enjoy vice, 'there springs in the conscience a displeasure that afflicts us sleeping and waking with various tormenting imaginations.' Examples/citations: Lucretius, Epicurus; the phenomenon appears as involuntary self-betrayal in dreams and sleeptalk. Use this to explain internal moral friction and its evidentiary force about a person's guilt or innocence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ill conscience produces fear; good conscience gives assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: A bad conscience fills a person with fear and inquietude, while a good conscience gives confidence and steadiness in hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne supports this with anecdotes about Scipio's calmness when accused and classical quotations (Ovid). He treats a steady, fearless demeanor as plausibly arising from knowledge of one's own innocence or from high spirit/fortune; use such examples to argue how internal moral state shows outward comportment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torture is a trial of patience, not of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of torturing suspects (the rack) is unreliable for establishing truth: it tests endurance more than factual guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne reasons that pain can force both innocent and guilty to speak — pain may make an innocent lie ('Pain will make even the innocent lie'), and the guilty may endure to preserve life. He cites historical trials (Philotas) and observes the extreme uncertainty and danger of torture as a means of proof. Anti-pattern: treating confessions under torture as reliable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is cruel and unjust to torture without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjecting a person to extreme examination before proof is more cruel and often worse than unjustly killing them without cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes many peoples' abhorrence of such practices and provides a military anecdote where a general rips open a soldier's belly to find if he stole soup — which produced a 'lesson' but highlights the barbarity. Use this to argue for restraint and the unjustness of preemptive cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (practice/experience) is necessary to translate knowledge into action
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument and instruction alone seldom lead to correct action; one must exercise and form the soul by experience to be ready when tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne draws on philosophers who voluntarily practised poverty, austerity, or hardships to prepare for fortune's trials. He states 'Use makes perfect' and recommends deliberate training/experience to avoid being 'surprised raw' by real difficulty. Application: emphasize experiential rehearsal alongside theoretical learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death cannot be fully practised but can be approached by analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Death itself can be experienced only once and so cannot be fully practised, but one may approach and familiarize oneself with it by analogies (sleep, swoon) and controlled hardships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that sleep resembles death and that swoons/near-death experiences give partial insight. He recounts his own swoon/fall as instructive in dimming fear of death. Use this to temper exaggerated dread while acknowledging limits of preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination exaggerates the intensity of future suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Things (illness, pain, death) often seem greater by imagination than they prove to be in reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne reports personal experience: robust health made sickness seem formidable, but actual sickness proved 'faint and easy' compared to imagined horrors. Use this to argue for restraint in anticipatory fear and the calibrating effect of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and describe oneself candidly
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-study and speaking of one's own thought and essence is a legitimate and necessary practice for understanding oneself; it is not automatically vain or presumptuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne defends writing about oneself against cultural proscriptions: he compares it to an architect speaking of building from his own knowledge. He acknowledges the risk of boasting but argues for impartial, truthful self-reporting as valuable material for inquiry. Anti-pattern: forbidding all self-discussion because some will boast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be impartial and truthful in self-assessment (neither under- nor over-state)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should value and report oneself cautiously and impartially: 'To speak less of one’s self than what one really is is folly... To speak more of one’s self than is really true... is often folly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites Aristotle and recommends avoiding both false modesty and indiscreet self-love. The safest course is an honest, balanced testimonial of one's qualities and defects; virtue does not need falsehood to assist it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride is primarily a matter of thought rather than outward speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride 'dwells in the thought; the tongue can have but a very little share in it' — thinking of oneself is not necessarily indulgence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne distinguishes internal self-regard from merely speaking of oneself; cultural prohibitions that try to stop both thinking and speaking of oneself are misguided. Encourage inward examination while guarding against self-exaltation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confession and self-accusation are part of honest self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Public or private self-disclosure may take the form of accusation of oneself; confessing faults is a part of honest self-study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes people confess to God or confessor and to neighbours; he claims his own writings are self-testimonies that may appear as accusations but are meant to reveal truth. Use candid admission of faults as a method of truthful self-portraiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honour's value derives from rarity; mixing honours with wealth debases them
rubrics_metrics.description: Recompenses of honour (crowns, titles, privileges) are valuable mainly because they are rare and non-material; if mixed with riches or made common, they lose their dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Augustus and the French Order of St. Michael as examples, Montaigne argues that honour should be a distinct, non-profitable acknowledgement of merit. Policy implication: design honours to be rare and symbolically distinct from material reward to preserve esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward virtue with appropriate (often non-monetary) recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is profitable and fitting to acknowledge rare merit with distinctions that cost little (garments, titles, precedence) rather than with money which is common and used for many ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne suggests honour is more flattering to the virtuous than money, which buys common services and can reward vice. When designing recompense systems, prefer symbolic distinctions for moral/elite recognition; beware turning honour into ordinary currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom's prohibitions can create perverse effects (overreaction against self-display)
rubrics_metrics.description: The social custom that condemns speaking of oneself can lead to excessive avoidance and to forbidding the necessary inspection of oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne labels cultural bans on self-discussion as making the remedy worse than the disease ('Instead of blowing the child’s nose, this is to take his nose off altogether'). He argues against absolute taboos and for measured, honest self-examination and reporting.
